Supervised Learning — Regression Algorithms¶

Logistic Regression (Credit Card Fraud Detection) & Linear Regression (Insurance Cost Prediction)¶

Supervised learning trains a model on examples whose correct answer (the label or target) is already known, so it can predict that answer for new, unseen data. The "regression" family covered here shares one idea: learn a weighted sum of the input features

$$z = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots + \beta_nx_n$$

and use it in two different ways:

Logistic Regression (Part A) Linear Regression (Part B)
Target type Category / class (fraud vs. not fraud) Continuous number (e.g. insurance cost)
Output $P(y=1) = \sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$ $\hat{y} = z$
Loss minimised Log-loss (cross-entropy) Mean squared error (ordinary least squares)
Typical metrics Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC R², MAE, RMSE

Despite its name, logistic regression is a classification algorithm: it squeezes the linear score through the sigmoid function to get a probability, then applies a threshold (0.5 by default) to decide the class.

Workflow followed in both parts

  1. Load the data and inspect its structure
  2. Preprocess: missing values, duplicates, encoding, scaling
  3. Exploratory data analysis (EDA)
  4. Split into train (70%) and test (30%)
  5. Train the model
  6. Evaluate on the unseen test set and interpret the results

Data files: download creditcard.csv (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mlg-ulb/creditcardfraud) and insurance.csv / insurance_2.csv (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mirichoi0218/insurance) and place them in the same folder as this notebook.

Part A — Credit Card Fraud Detection with Logistic Regression¶

Problem statement: Using the Kaggle Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset, build a machine-learning model that detects whether a credit card transaction is fraudulent. Demonstrate data preprocessing and analysis, split the data into train (0.7) and test (0.3), build the model with logistic regression, and evaluate its accuracy.

About the data: transactions made by European cardholders over two days in September 2013.

  • Time – seconds elapsed since the first transaction in the dataset
  • V1 … V28 – anonymised features produced by a PCA transformation (the original features are confidential)
  • Amount – transaction amount
  • Class – target: 1 = fraud, 0 = genuine

A.2 Data preprocessing — missing values and duplicates¶

In [29]:
print("Missing values in the whole dataset:", int(cc.isnull().sum().sum()))
n_dup = cc.duplicated().sum()
print("Duplicate rows:", n_dup)

cc = cc.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)
print("Shape after removing duplicates:", cc.shape)

Missing values in the whole dataset: 0
Duplicate rows: 1081
Shape after removing duplicates: (283726, 31)

Why remove duplicates?

Identical rows could land in both the training and test sets, letting the model be "tested" on rows it has already seen (data leakage). That would inflate the scores and give those rows extra weight in training.

A.3 Exploratory data analysis¶

Target distribution — how imbalanced is the problem?¶

Why a log scale?

Genuine transactions outnumber frauds about 600 to 1, so on a normal axis the fraud bar would be invisible. The log scale keeps both bars visible, and the labels above them show the true counts.

In [30]:
counts = cc["Class"].value_counts().sort_index()
pct = cc["Class"].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index() * 100
class_table = pd.DataFrame({"Transactions": counts, "Percent (%)": pct})
class_table.index = ["Genuine (0)", "Fraud (1)"]
print(class_table)
print(f"\nImbalance ratio: about 1 fraud for every {counts[0] // counts[1]} genuine transactions")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
bars = ax.bar(class_table.index, class_table["Transactions"], color=[BLUE, ORANGE], width=0.5)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of transactions (log scale)")
ax.set_title("Class distribution: fraud is extremely rare")
for b, n, p in zip(bars, class_table["Transactions"], class_table["Percent (%)"]):
    ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, n * 1.15, f"{n:,}\n({p:.2f}%)", ha="center", va="bottom")
ax.set_ylim(100, 2e6)

A.4 Train / test split (70 / 30) and feature scaling¶

  • stratify=y keeps the same (tiny) fraud percentage in both train and test sets; without it the test set could end up with too few frauds to evaluate reliably.
  • V1–V28 are already PCA outputs, but Time and Amount are on very different scales. Logistic regression is fitted with gradient-based optimisation and L2 regularisation, both of which work best when features are on comparable scales, so all features are standardised.
  • The scaler is fitted on the training set only and then applied to the test set, so no information from the test data leaks into training.
In [34]:
X = cc.drop(columns="Class")
y = cc["Class"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_s = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_s = scaler.transform(X_test)

print(f"Training set: {X_train.shape[0]:,} rows  |  frauds: {y_train.sum():,} ({y_train.mean()*100:.3f}%)")
print(f"Test set:     {X_test.shape[0]:,} rows  |  frauds: {y_test.sum():,} ({y_test.mean()*100:.3f}%)")

Training set: 198,608 rows  |  frauds: 331 (0.167%)
Test set:     85,118 rows  |  frauds: 142 (0.167%)

A.5 Build the logistic regression model¶

In [35]:
log_reg = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
log_reg.fit(X_train_s, y_train)

y_train_pred = log_reg.predict(X_train_s)
y_test_pred = log_reg.predict(X_test_s)
y_test_proba = log_reg.predict_proba(X_test_s)[:, 1]

train_acc = accuracy_score(y_train, y_train_pred)
test_acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_test_pred)
print(f"Training accuracy: {train_acc*100:.3f}%")
print(f"Test accuracy:     {test_acc*100:.3f}%")

Training accuracy: 99.922%
Test accuracy:     99.908%

A.6 Evaluate the model¶

Is accuracy enough? Compare against a "do-nothing" baseline¶

A model that always predicts "genuine" never catches a single fraud, yet it scores very high accuracy because 99.8% of transactions are genuine. Any fraud model must therefore be judged with metrics that focus on the fraud class as well.

In [36]:
baseline_acc = (y_test == 0).mean()
print(f"Baseline accuracy (always predict 'genuine'): {baseline_acc*100:.3f}%")
print(f"Logistic regression accuracy:                 {test_acc*100:.3f}%")
print(f"Improvement over baseline: {(test_acc - baseline_acc)*100:.3f} percentage points")

Baseline accuracy (always predict 'genuine'): 99.833%
Logistic regression accuracy:                 99.908%
Improvement over baseline: 0.075 percentage points

print(f"ROC-AUC:                     {roc_auc_score(y_test, y_test_proba):.4f}")

Additional experiment — handling class imbalance with class_weight="balanced"¶

The default model treats every mistake equally, so with so few frauds it leans towards predicting "genuine". Setting class_weight="balanced" makes each fraud example count roughly 600× more (the inverse of its frequency) in the loss. This shows the trade-off between catching frauds (recall) and raising false alarms (precision).

In [40]:
log_reg_bal = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
log_reg_bal.fit(X_train_s, y_train)
y_pred_bal = log_reg_bal.predict(X_test_s)
proba_bal = log_reg_bal.predict_proba(X_test_s)[:, 1]

def summarise(name, y_true, y_pred, y_proba):
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel()
    return {"Model": name, "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
            "Precision (fraud)": precision_score(y_true, y_pred), "Recall (fraud)": recall_score(y_true, y_pred),
            "F1 (fraud)": f1_score(y_true, y_pred), "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_true, y_proba),
            "Frauds caught": tp, "Frauds missed": fn, "False alarms": fp}

comparison_a = pd.DataFrame([
    summarise("Logistic regression (default)", y_test, y_test_pred, y_test_proba),
    summarise("Logistic regression (balanced weights)", y_test, y_pred_bal, proba_bal),
]).set_index("Model")
comparison_a

A.7 Part A — Findings¶

Data and preprocessing

  • The dataset has 284,807 transactions and 31 columns with no missing values. 1,081 duplicate rows were removed, leaving 283,726.
  • The classes are extremely imbalanced: only 473 frauds (0.167%), about 1 fraud for every 598 genuine transactions. A stratified 70/30 split kept that ratio in both sets (331 frauds in training, 142 in test).
  • Fraudulent transactions have a lower median amount ($9.82 vs $22.00) but a higher mean, so fraud includes many small "test" charges plus some larger ones.
  • The PCA features V17, V14, V12 and V10 have the strongest (negative) correlation with fraud, and V11 and V4 the strongest positive correlation. Their distributions clearly separate the two classes, which is why a linear model can work well here.

Model performance (test set, 85,118 transactions)

  • Accuracy = 99.91% (training 99.92%, so there is no sign of overfitting).
  • That figure has to be read in context: a model that always says "genuine" already scores 99.83%. The real gain is only 0.075 percentage points, so accuracy on its own is a misleading metric for imbalanced data.
  • The fraud-focused metrics give a truer picture:
    • Precision 0.84: when the model raises an alert, it is right 84% of the time (only 15 false alarms).
    • Recall 0.56: it catches 79 of 142 frauds but misses 63.
    • F1 = 0.67, ROC-AUC = 0.965, PR-AUC = 0.70. The model ranks transactions by risk very well, but the default 0.5 threshold is cautious about flagging fraud.
  • The most influential features are V4 (raises fraud risk) and V14 and V10 (lower values point strongly to fraud), consistent with the correlation analysis.

Imbalance experiment

  • With class_weight="balanced", recall jumps from 56% to 89% (126 of 142 frauds caught), but false alarms rise from 15 to 2,267 and accuracy drops to 97.3%. ROC-AUC barely changes (0.965 → 0.966), which shows the ranking ability is the same; only the trade-off point moves.
  • Which model is "better" depends on the business cost of a missed fraud versus a blocked genuine customer. In practice, tuning the decision threshold, resampling (e.g. SMOTE) or non-linear models (e.g. gradient boosting) would be the next steps.

Part B — Insurance Cost Prediction with Linear Regression¶

Problem statement: Using the Kaggle Medical Cost Personal (insurance) dataset, build a predictive system to predict insurance costs. Demonstrate data preprocessing and analysis, split the data into train (0.7) and test (0.3), build the model with linear regression, and evaluate how accurately it predicts insurance cost.

About the data:

  • age – age of the primary beneficiary
  • sex – female / male
  • bmi – body mass index (kg/m²); 18.5–24.9 is the healthy range
  • children – number of dependants covered by the plan
  • smoker – yes / no
  • region – US residential area: northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest
  • charges – target: individual medical costs billed by the insurer (USD)

B.4 Encode categorical variables¶

Linear regression needs numeric inputs.

  • sex and smoker have two values each, so they become 0/1 columns (male, smoker).
  • region has four unordered values, so it is one-hot encoded. One column (northeast) is dropped and acts as the reference category; keeping all four would make them perfectly collinear with the intercept (the "dummy variable trap").
In [50]:

ins_enc["smoker"] = (ins_enc["smoker"] == "yes").astype(int)
ins_enc = pd.get_dummies(ins_enc, columns=["region"], drop_first=True, dtype=int)

B.5 Train / test split (70 / 30)¶

Ordinary least squares linear regression is not affected by feature scale (the coefficients simply adjust), so the features are left in their original units. That keeps the coefficients directly readable as dollars per unit.

In [52]:

Reading the coefficients: holding everything else constant, each coefficient is the change in predicted annual charges for a one-unit increase in that feature, e.g. the smoker coefficient is the extra cost of being a smoker compared with a non-smoker with the same age, BMI, etc.

B.7 Evaluate the model¶

For a regression model "accuracy" is measured by how close predictions are to the true values:

  • R² – share of the variation in charges that the model explains (1.0 = perfect)
  • MAE – average absolute error in dollars
  • RMSE – root mean squared error in dollars (penalises large misses more)
In [54]:
yi_train_pred = lin_reg.predict(Xi_train)
yi_test_pred = lin_reg.predict(Xi_test)

def reg_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    return {"R²": r2_score(y_true, y_pred),
            "MAE (USD)": mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred),
            "RMSE (USD)": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))}

metrics_b = pd.DataFrame({"Train": reg_metrics(yi_train, yi_train_pred),
                          "Test": reg_metrics(yi_test, yi_test_pred)}).T
print(f"The model explains {metrics_b.loc['Test', 'R²']*100:.1f}% of the variance in insurance charges on unseen test data.")

cv_r2 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), Xi_train, yi_train, cv=5, scoring="r2")
print(f"5-fold cross-validated R² on the training set: {cv_r2.mean():.4f} ± {cv_r2.std():.4f}")

B.8 The predictive system¶

A small function wraps the trained model so it can predict the cost for a new person from raw, human-readable inputs.

In [56]:
def predict_insurance_cost(age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, region, model=lin_reg, columns=X_ins.columns):
    # Predict annual insurance charges (USD) for one person.
    row = {"age": age, "male": int(sex == "male"), "bmi": bmi, "children": children,
           "smoker": int(smoker == "yes"),
           "region_northwest": int(region == "northwest"),
           "region_southeast": int(region == "southeast"),
           "region_southwest": int(region == "southwest")}
    return float(model.predict(pd.DataFrame([row])[columns])[0])

examples = pd.DataFrame([
    dict(age=31, sex="female", bmi=25.7, children=0, smoker="no", region="southeast"),
    dict(age=31, sex="female", bmi=25.7, children=0, smoker="yes", region="southeast"),
    dict(age=52, sex="male", bmi=34.1, children=2, smoker="no", region="northwest"),
    dict(age=52, sex="male", bmi=34.1, children=2, smoker="yes", region="northwest"),
])
examples["Predicted charges (USD)"] = [predict_insurance_cost(**r) for r in examples.to_dict("records")]
examples.style.format({"Predicted charges (USD)": "${:,.2f}", "bmi": "{:.1f}"})

Additional experiment — improving the linear model with feature engineering¶

The EDA showed two patterns that a plain straight-line model cannot capture: charges for smokers jump sharply once BMI exceeds 30, and cost grows faster at older ages. Linear regression is still linear in its coefficients, so we can add engineered features and keep the same algorithm:

  • obese = 1 if BMI ≥ 30
  • smoker_obese = smoker × obese (interaction)
  • age_sq = age² (curvature)
In [58]:
def add_features(df):
    df = df.copy()
    df["obese"] = (df["bmi"] >= 30).astype(int)
    df["smoker_obese"] = df["smoker"] * df["obese"]
    df["age_sq"] = df["age"] ** 2
    return df

Xf_train, Xf_test = add_features(Xi_train), add_features(Xi_test)
lin_reg_fe = LinearRegression().fit(Xf_train, yi_train)
yf_test_pred = lin_reg_fe.predict(Xf_test)

comparison_b = pd.DataFrame({
    "Baseline linear regression": reg_metrics(yi_test, yi_test_pred),
    "With engineered features": reg_metrics(yi_test, yf_test_pred),
}).T
print("Test-set comparison:")
comparison_b

B.9 Part B — Findings¶

Data and preprocessing

  • The dataset has 1,338 records and 7 columns with no missing values. One duplicate row was removed (1,337 remain).
  • sex and smoker were binary-encoded and region was one-hot encoded (northeast as reference). The data was split 70/30 (935 train, 402 test).
  • charges is right-skewed (mean $13,279 vs median $9,386): most people have modest costs and a minority have very high costs.

What drives insurance cost (EDA)

  • Smoking is by far the strongest factor (correlation 0.79). Smokers average $32,050** against **$8,441 for non-smokers, almost 4× higher.
  • Age is the second driver (correlation 0.30): charges rise steadily with age in three bands (non-smokers, a mixed middle band, and smokers).
  • BMI matters mostly through its interaction with smoking: smokers with BMI ≥ 30 form a distinct high-cost group (around $40k and above).
  • Sex, region and number of children have only small effects.

Linear regression model

  • Fitted coefficients: being a smoker adds about $22,874**, each extra **year of age adds about $251, each BMI point adds about $328**, and each **child adds about $522. Sex and region shift costs by less than $1,000.
  • Test R² = 0.772: the model explains 77.2% of the variation in insurance charges on unseen data. MAE ≈ $4,182** and **RMSE ≈ $6,240.
  • Training R² (0.736) and 5-fold cross-validated R² (0.729 ± 0.031) are close to the test score, so the model generalises well and is not overfitting.
  • The residual plot shows clear structure: the model under-predicts obese smokers and over-predicts some non-obese smokers, because a single straight line cannot represent the smoker × BMI jump.

Improving the model

  • Adding three engineered features (obese, smoker × obese, age²) while keeping linear regression raised test R² from 0.772 to 0.875 and cut MAE from $4,182 to $2,515 (about 40% lower). Good feature engineering based on EDA can matter more than switching algorithms.
  • The predict_insurance_cost() function turns the trained model into a usable predictive system: for example, a 31-year-old non-smoking woman versus an otherwise identical smoker differ by about $22,900 in predicted cost.

Overall conclusion¶

Part A — Logistic Regression Part B — Linear Regression
Task Classify a transaction as fraud / genuine Predict a continuous cost in USD
Headline result Accuracy 99.91% (ROC-AUC 0.965) R² 0.772 (0.875 with engineered features)
Key lesson Accuracy is misleading with imbalanced classes; precision, recall and the confusion matrix tell the real story Linear models are easy to interpret; EDA-driven features capture non-linear effects

Both algorithms learn a weighted sum of the inputs. Linear regression uses it directly as the prediction, while logistic regression passes it through a sigmoid to produce a probability. Both are fast, interpretable baselines: their coefficients show which features matter and in which direction. Their limits (a single linear decision boundary, no automatic interactions) appeared in both parts, and were addressed by rebalancing the classes in Part A and by feature engineering in Part B.
